question: Which property most directly distinguishes a conventional array from a linked list?

options.text: Insertion at every position takes constant time
Every element must have a different data type
Elements are stored in contiguous memory locations
The structure cannot be traversed sequentially

explanation: Conventional arrays store elements contiguously, enabling direct index-based access.

question: For an array declared with capacity 20 and currently containing 13 valid elements, which statement is correct?

options.text: Its length and capacity must both be 13
Its length is 13 and its capacity is 20
Its length is 20 and its capacity is 13
Its length is 7 and its capacity is 20

explanation: Length counts valid elements; capacity is the maximum number that can be stored without resizing.

question: Which operation on a conventional array is typically Θ(1) when the index is valid?

options.text: Deleting an element from the middle
Inserting at the beginning
Accessing an element by index
Searching for an arbitrary value

explanation: Index-based access is constant time; shifting for insertion/deletion can take linear time.

question: A fixed-size array has capacity 10 and currently stores 10 elements. What is generally required to append one more element?

options.text: Converting every element to a linked-list node
Nothing; arrays automatically grow in every language
Only sorting the array first
A larger backing array or a different data structure

explanation: A full fixed-capacity array cannot accept another element unless storage is expanded or the representation changes.

question: Which statement about arrays is generally true?

options.text: Arrays can only store numeric values
Direct indexed access is efficient, but middle insertions may require shifting
Array elements are normally scattered arbitrarily through memory
All array operations are Θ(1)

explanation: Arrays trade efficient indexing for potentially costly insertion/deletion away from the end.

question: In a zero-based array of length n, which index is the last valid index when n > 0?

options.text: n

explanation: Zero-based indices run from 0 through n−1.

question: A one-dimensional array contains 8 elements. Which access is out of bounds under zero-based indexing?
explanation: For length 8, valid indices are 0 through 7.

question: Which best describes a multidimensional array?

options.text: An array that cannot store numeric values
A collection that must have unequal row lengths
An array organized using more than one index dimension
An array whose elements are always linked nodes

explanation: A two-dimensional array, for example, is indexed by row and column.

question: Which statement about a two-dimensional array is correct in the abstract model?

options.text: It can contain only square matrices
An element is identified using row and column indices
It is always stored as a linked list
Every matrix operation must be Θ(n)

explanation: A 2D array is accessed using two indices, though physical storage layout depends on the language/representation.

question: What is the main limitation of a conventional fixed-size static array?

options.text: It does not support indexed access
It cannot be traversed
Its size cannot be changed after allocation in the usual fixed-array model
It must contain duplicate values

explanation: Fixed-size arrays may waste unused capacity or run out of space when the required size changes.

question: Which statement best distinguishes a dynamic array from a fixed-size array?

options.text: A dynamic array never uses contiguous memory
A dynamic array can grow its backing storage, often by allocating and copying
A dynamic array cannot be indexed
A dynamic array always provides Θ(1) insertion at every position

explanation: Dynamic arrays commonly resize when capacity is reached; an individual resize can be expensive.

question: In a typical dynamic array, appending one element has which usual complexity claim over a long sequence of appends?

options.text: Θ(n²) total for n appends
Θ(log n) worst case for every append
Θ(1) amortized per append
Θ(n) amortized per append

explanation: Geometric resizing makes total work over n appends Θ(n), so amortized append cost is Θ(1).

question: What is the typical time complexity of traversing all n elements of an array once?

options.text: Θ(n)
Θ(n²)
Θ(log n)

explanation: Each element is visited once, producing linear work.

question: Inserting an element at index 0 into an array of n valid elements usually takes:

options.text: Θ(log n)
Θ(n²)
Θ(1), regardless of n
Θ(n), because elements may need to shift

explanation: Existing elements generally need to be shifted one position to make room.

question: Deleting an element from the middle of a packed array usually requires:

options.text: Rebuilding the entire computer memory
Shifting later elements left to preserve packed order
No changes to any other element
Sorting the array in descending order

explanation: In a packed array, later elements are moved left to close the gap.

question: Which statement about updating A[i] when i is a valid index is usually correct?

options.text: It requires a linear search in every array implementation
It always resizes the array
It is Θ(1) when the index is already known
It is Θ(n²)

explanation: Replacing a known indexed element is a constant-time operation.

question: Searching for a value in an unsorted array using a simple sequential scan has worst-case time:

options.text: Θ(n)
Θ(log n)
Θ(n log n)

explanation: The value may be at the end or absent, requiring inspection of all n elements.

question: Binary search is directly applicable to which array condition?

options.text: The array is stored in reverse memory order
The array has an even number of elements
The array has no duplicate values
The array is sorted according to the searched ordering

explanation: Binary search relies on sorted order to discard half the remaining search interval.

question: What is the time complexity of deleting the last element from a dynamic array when no resizing or extra work is triggered?

options.text: Θ(n²)
Θ(log n)
Θ(n)

explanation: Removing the final logical element typically only changes the stored length.

question: Which is the most accurate complexity summary for a conventional array of n elements?

options.text: Index access Θ(n), search Θ(1), insertion Θ(log n)
Every operation is Θ(n)
Index access Θ(log n), traversal Θ(1), deletion Θ(1)
Index access Θ(1), traversal Θ(n), middle insertion Θ(n)

explanation: These are typical bounds for direct access, a full scan, and insertion requiring shifts.

question: Which traversal visits array elements in their stored order from the first index to the last?

options.text: Forward traversal
Binary traversal
Randomized traversal
Reverse traversal

explanation: Forward traversal processes indices in increasing order.

question: A matrix has 4 rows and 6 columns. How many elements does it contain?
explanation: A rectangular matrix with r rows and c columns contains r × c elements.

question: For matrices A and B of the same dimensions, matrix addition is performed by:

options.text: Transposing A and then ignoring B
Adding row indices and column indices only
Multiplying every element of A by every element of B
Adding corresponding elements at the same row and column positions

explanation: Matrix addition is element-wise and requires equal dimensions.

question: If A is an r × c matrix and B is a c × p matrix, the product AB has dimensions:

options.text: r × p
p × r
r × c
c × c

explanation: For AB, the inner dimensions c must match; the product has the outer dimensions r × p.

question: Which condition is required for the product AB to be defined?

options.text: The number of rows of A equals the number of rows of B
A and B must both be square and the same size
A and B must be symmetric
The number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B

explanation: Matrix multiplication is defined when A's column count equals B's row count.

question: If A is an r × c matrix, what are the dimensions of its transpose Aᵀ?

options.text: c × r
r × r
c × c
r × c

explanation: Transpose interchanges rows and columns.

question: Which statement about matrix multiplication is generally correct?

options.text: Every matrix commutes with every other matrix of compatible dimensions
AB is defined exactly when BA is defined
AB always equals BA
Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative

explanation: In general AB ≠ BA, and the two products may even differ in whether they are defined.

question: A square matrix is symmetric if:

options.text: All entries above the main diagonal are zero
It equals its transpose
Its diagonal entries are all distinct
All its entries are zero

explanation: A symmetric matrix satisfies A = Aᵀ, so corresponding entries across the main diagonal match.

question: In a square upper triangular matrix, which entries must be zero?

options.text: All entries below the main diagonal
All entries in the first row
All entries above the main diagonal
All entries on the main diagonal

explanation: An upper triangular matrix has zeros strictly below the main diagonal.

question: In a square lower triangular matrix, which entries must be zero?

options.text: All entries in the last row
All entries strictly above the main diagonal
All entries strictly below the main diagonal
All diagonal entries

explanation: A lower triangular matrix has zeros strictly above the main diagonal.

question: A diagonal matrix is a square matrix in which:

options.text: Every entry is nonzero
Every row contains exactly one nonzero entry
All entries outside the main diagonal are zero
All diagonal entries are equal to 1

explanation: A diagonal matrix permits nonzero values on the main diagonal and has zeros elsewhere.

question: Which statement about a diagonal matrix is true?

options.text: It is both upper and lower triangular
It must contain only zeroes
It must be non-square
It cannot be an identity matrix

explanation: A diagonal matrix has zeros both above and below the diagonal, satisfying both triangular conditions.

question: A sparse matrix is generally one that:

options.text: Must be square and symmetric
Has mostly zero entries
Has exactly one nonzero entry in every row
Has no zero entries

explanation: Sparse matrices contain relatively few nonzero values compared with the total number of entries.

question: Why can compact storage be useful for a sparse matrix?

options.text: It stores only nonzero values and their locations, reducing wasted space
It converts every sparse matrix into a diagonal matrix
It makes every matrix operation constant time
It increases the number of zero values

explanation: Sparse formats avoid storing many zeros explicitly, though operations depend on the format and sparsity pattern.

question: In a common triplet representation of a sparse matrix, each stored entry records:

options.text: The row sum, column sum, and determinant
Row index, column index, and nonzero value
Only the diagonal entries
Only the value, without its position

explanation: A triplet typically stores (row, column, value) for each nonzero element, sometimes with a header for dimensions/count.

question: A matrix has 100 × 100 entries but only 8 nonzero values. Which representation is likely to use less storage for the values, assuming modest index overhead?

options.text: A transpose, because transposition removes zeros
A full dense array in all circumstances
A sparse representation storing nonzero values and their coordinates
A triangular representation, because every sparse matrix is triangular

explanation: With very few nonzero values, triplet or another sparse format can use far less storage than all 10,000 entries.

question: How many entries are on or above the main diagonal of an n × n upper triangular matrix?

options.text: 2n
n²

explanation: There are n entries in the first row on/above the diagonal, n−1 in the next, and so on: n(n+1)/2 total.

question: How many entries are strictly above the main diagonal of an n × n matrix?

options.text: n
n²

question: Which is a realistic application of matrices in data representation?

options.text: Representing a grayscale image as rows and columns of pixel intensities
Ensuring all data are stored in alphabetical order
Eliminating the need for indexing
Representing every linked list as one scalar only

explanation: Images, tables, adjacency matrices, and numerical data are common matrix applications.

question: An adjacency matrix for a simple graph with n vertices uses how many matrix entries?

options.text: n
2n
n²

explanation: An adjacency matrix is n × n, with one entry for each ordered pair of vertices.

question: Which operation is usually Θ(r c) for two dense matrices of the same r × c dimensions?

options.text: Changing one element
Adding the matrices
Finding a single element by index
Reading one known element

explanation: Addition processes each of the rc corresponding positions once.

question: For standard multiplication of an r × c matrix by a c × p matrix, the basic algorithm takes:

options.text: Θ(r c p)
Θ(r p) in all cases regardless of c
Θ(log(rcp))
Θ(r + c + p)

explanation: The standard triple-loop method performs work proportional to r × c × p.

question: Which statement about matrix transpose is correct for a dense r × c matrix when constructing a new matrix?

options.text: It requires Θ(r²c²) time
It usually visits all rc elements, so Θ(rc) time
It is always Θ(1)
It is impossible unless the matrix is square

explanation: Every element must be placed at its swapped row/column position.

question: Which is a common in-place array problem pattern that can be solved with two pointers?

options.text: Computing every permutation of n distinct elements
Listing all subsets of a set
Finding a pair in a sorted array whose sum equals a target
Multiplying any two rectangular matrices

explanation: Two pointers can move inward based on the current sum in a sorted array.

question: Which technique is often used to answer many range-sum queries efficiently on a static array?

options.text: Using only a stack and discarding all values
Prefix sums
Replacing the array with a single maximum value
Repeatedly sort the array before every query

explanation: Prefix sums allow a range sum to be computed from two prefix values in constant time after linear preprocessing.

question: For a fixed-size array, which statement about deleting an element is the best general answer when preserving order?

options.text: Only the logical length changes; all later elements stay in place
The array automatically becomes a linked list
It always takes Θ(log n)
Later elements may need to shift left, taking Θ(n) time in the worst case

explanation: Maintaining packed order requires shifting later elements after deletion.

question: An array has length 12 and capacity 16. After deleting 3 elements, assuming no shrinking policy, what are its length and capacity?

options.text: Length 9, capacity 12
Length 9, capacity 16
Length 16, capacity 9
Length 12, capacity 13

explanation: Deletion reduces the number of valid elements; capacity remains 16 if the implementation does not shrink.

question: Which statement about duplicates in an array is correct?

options.text: Duplicate values may occur unless a separate constraint forbids them
Arrays cannot contain duplicate values
A duplicate value automatically changes the array into a set
Duplicates make indexed access impossible

explanation: Arrays generally permit repeated values; uniqueness is a property of an application or data structure contract.

question: A row-major representation of a matrix stores:

options.text: Only diagonal elements
Only nonzero entries
All elements of the first column, then the second column, and so on
All elements of the first row, then the second row, and so on

explanation: Row-major layout places consecutive rows consecutively in memory; exact layout is language-dependent.

question: Which statement about array-based problem solving is most accurate?

options.text: Sorting is unnecessary before binary search in every case
A sliding window can only be used with matrices
Prefix sums, sliding windows, and two pointers are reusable patterns for suitable array problems
Two pointers always work on unsorted arrays for every target-sum problem

explanation: These are common patterns, but each has preconditions; for example, two-pointer target-sum often relies on sorted order.
